953.title: Moroccan scholarship
953.hook: Fez and Marrakesh as cities of scholars, Sufis and craftsmen
953.howItsDone: In Fez and Marrakesh, historic madrasahs, mosques and saints' tombs are still visited, students still study at al-Qarawiyyin, and crafts such as zellij tilework are still practiced and taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Almoravids and Almohads, two strict movements of renewal that ruled North Africa and al-Andalus in turn. Your line was: renewal from the desert. What did you begin again? Day nine hundred fifty-three.

Tap, tap, tap. In a workshop in Fez, a craftsman holds a small hammer and a square of glazed tile, and chips it into a tiny shape, a star point, a curved petal. Piece after piece will be laid face down, fitted together like a puzzle, and set in plaster, until they become a wall that glitters. Across the lane, in the courtyard of a college, students sit reading. The tiles around them were cut by hands like his. In the old cities of Morocco, the scholar and the craftsman worked within a few steps of each other. Today: Moroccan scholarship.
screen: `TAP, TAP — A TILE IS CUT.` → `A PUZZLE BECOMES A WALL.` → `THE SCHOLAR AND THE CRAFTSMAN.`

segments.voice: In Fez, the city's learning gathered around the mosque of al-Qarawiyyin, founded, as the chronicle you heard last week tells it, by Fatimah al-Fihri. Around it, rulers and donors added madrasahs: courtyards with a fountain, rooms for students upstairs, a prayer hall, and walls covered in carved cedar, carved plaster and tilework. Marrakesh, founded by the Almoravids, became another city of learning in the south, with its own mosques, colleges and markets. In both, learning wasn't shut away. It lived next to the tanneries and the copper beaters and the book binders. Marrakesh also honors a group that tradition calls its seven saints, and the list joins two kinds of learning. One is Qadi Iyad, a judge and a scholar of hadith and law. Another is al-Jazuli, a Sufi whose book of blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still recited. A judge and a mystic, side by side, honored by the same city. And the craftsmen? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 2072, says that nobody has eaten better food than what they earn by the work of their own hands, and that the prophet David ate from the work of his hands. Work with the hands wasn't a step down from study. It was honored too. So when someone says Moroccan scholarship, the picture is wider than a man with a book. It's the book, the student's room, the cut tile on the wall, the saint's tomb at the end of the lane. Cities of learning.
screen: `FEZ AROUND THE QARAWIYYIN.` · `MADRASAHS OF CEDAR, PLASTER, TILE.` · `A JUDGE AND A MYSTIC, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE WORK OF YOUR OWN HANDS.` · then, large: `CITIES OF LEARNING.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn a craft word. Here's one from Morocco: zellij, the cut glazed tilework from the hook. Settle, and breathe. Say it quietly: zellij. Now look at your own hands. Think of one thing they know how to make or mend: bread, a shelf, a stitch, a garden bed, a careful page of handwriting. Hold that skill in mind the way a scholar holds a text. If you pray, you can give thanks for the work of your hands. If you don't, simply notice what your hands can do. The bell holds the time.
Moroccan scholarship. Fez and Marrakesh as cities where scholars, Sufis and craftsmen lived and worked within a few steps of each other. Today's word.
Your line: cities of learning. Today, learn the name of one craft from someone who does it, and ask them one question about how it's done. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: The Maghreb's Maliki school
954.hook: the Maliki school of law becomes the tradition of North and West Africa
954.carry: the school of medina traveled west
954.howItsDone: The Maliki school is followed in North and West Africa, the Muwatta of Imam Malik is still studied, and some Maliki worshippers pray with their arms at their sides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moroccan scholarship: Fez and Marrakesh, where scholars, Sufis and craftsmen shared the same lanes. Your line was: cities of learning. Did you learn a craft word? Day nine hundred fifty-four.

A caliph has a book he admires, a collection of hadith and legal rulings by a scholar in Medina. He makes an offer: let this be the law for every land, copied out and sent to every city, so everyone follows one book. The scholar who wrote it says no. The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he answers, scattered to many lands, and the people there have learned from them. Let them keep what they have. That's how tradition tells it, and the scholar was Malik ibn Anas. His book stayed one voice among several. And yet it traveled further west than he ever did. Today: the Maghreb's Maliki school.
screen: `ONE BOOK FOR EVERY LAND?` → `THE SCHOLAR SAYS NO.` → `HIS BOOK TRAVELS WEST ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Malik lived and taught in Medina, the Prophet's own city. His book is the Muwatta, a title that can be rendered the well-trodden path, the way already smoothed by feet. What made his method his own was this: alongside the Qur'an and the hadith, he gave great weight to the practice of the people of Medina, what the community there actually did, handed down from the generation that had lived beside the Prophet. If Medina still did it, that counted as evidence. Students came to Medina, heard the Muwatta from Malik, and carried it home. Some went west. In Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, scholars gathered his teaching into great law books. In al-Andalus, a student's copy of the Muwatta became the version people learned. From there the school spread through the Maghreb, and along the trade routes south across the Sahara into West Africa. Yesterday's Qadi Iyad, one of the seven saints of Marrakesh, was a Maliki judge. The Almoravids, two days ago, held to Maliki law closely. That's today's line: the school of medina traveled west. One visible sign you may notice: some Malikis pray with their arms at their sides rather than folded. A Maliki is not a different kind of Muslim. The schools of Sunni law, the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali, share the same Qur'an and prayers, and differ in method and detail. Sunni scholars have long treated the four as ways of reading the same sources, not rival faiths. Shia Muslims have their own schools of law, such as the Ja'fari. That closes this stretch on Cairo, the Maghreb and the scholars.
screen: `MALIK OF MEDINA.` · `THE MUWATTA — THE WELL-TRODDEN PATH.` · `KAIROUAN, AL-ANDALUS, WEST AFRICA.` · `SCHOOLS DIFFER IN METHOD, NOT FAITH.` · then, large: `THE SCHOOL OF MEDINA TRAVELED WEST.`

segments.voice: The practice: find out which school of law is common near you. For the sit, settle and breathe. Think of the mosque nearest to you, or a Muslim friend or neighbor, or the country your family comes from, if that's your story. Do you know which school they follow? If you don't, that's the question to carry. Then bring to mind Malik's answer to the caliph: let the people keep what they learned. If you pray, you can ask for respect for those who pray a little differently. If you don't, simply hold that picture of one path walked in many ways. The bell holds the time.
The Maghreb's Maliki school. The way of law taught by Malik of Medina, which traveled west and took root in North and West Africa. Today's word.
Your line: the school of medina traveled west. Today, ask someone, or look up, which school of law is followed in a mosque near you. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

955.title: Jerusalem, 1099
955.hook: the First Crusade takes Jerusalem with great slaughter
955.howItsDone: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (we are God's, and to Him we return) at news of a death or loss, and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem is honored as the place of the Night Journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maghreb's Maliki school, carried west from Medina by Malik's students. Your line was: the school of medina traveled west. Did you find out which school is followed near you? Day nine hundred fifty-five.

A group of refugees reaches Baghdad in the month of Ramadan. They have come a long way, from Syria and from Jerusalem. A judge brings them into the caliph's court, and they tell what they saw. The chronicler Ibn al-Athir says their story brought tears to the eyes of those who heard it. Then he adds a line about the rulers: they were divided among themselves, and nothing was done. This part of the path turns to the Crusades, the Mongols and the Mamluks. It starts with the city those refugees had fled. Today: Jerusalem.
screen: `REFUGEES REACH BAGHDAD.` → `THE COURT WEEPS.` → `THE RULERS ARE DIVIDED.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem matters in Islam because of a journey. The Qur'an opens one of its surahs with it. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship the neighbourhood whereof We have blessed." Muslims understand the Far Distant Place of Worship, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, to be in Jerusalem, and tradition says believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the Ka'bah. So it was holy ground, shared in different ways with Jews and Christians, who hold it holy too. Armies from western Europe, the Franks of the First Crusade, marched a long way to take it. When the city fell, they killed a great many of the people inside. Muslim chroniclers like Ibn al-Athir describe killing in the Aqsa mosque itself, among scholars and devout people who had come to live near it. Another chronicler of Damascus, Ibn al-Qalanisi, writes that Jews were burned in their synagogue. Chroniclers among the Franks recorded the killing too. Nobody's numbers can be trusted, so we won't give any. The Qur'an gives words for a moment of loss like this. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Those words are still said at news of a loss. Jerusalem, for a long time after, was a city in grief. And the refugees in Baghdad had named the problem the next generations would have to answer: a divided people.
screen: `THE NIGHT JOURNEY TO AL-AQSA.` · `HOLY GROUND, SHARED IN MANY WAYS.` · `THE CITY FALLS, THE KILLING BEGINS.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND UNTO HIM RETURNING.` · then, large: `A CITY IN GRIEF.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember all who died there. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind the city that day: Muslims in the mosque, Jews in their synagogue, people of every faith in the streets, soldiers on every side. You don't need faces or numbers. Just hold them, all of them, as people. If you pray, you can pray for all who died there, and you can say the words the Qur'an gives for loss: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we are God's, and to Him we return. If you don't pray, simply keep a silence for them. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem. The city of the Night Journey and the Aqsa mosque, holy to Muslims, Jews and Christians, and the city taken with great slaughter in the First Crusade. Today's word.
Your line: a city in grief. Today, when you hear news of a place in pain, stop for one breath and remember the people, not the numbers. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Salah al-Din
956.hook: the Kurdish sultan who united Egypt and Syria
956.howItsDone: Salah al-Din's tomb in Damascus is still visited, and Ibn Shaddad's biography of him is still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem, taken in the First Crusade, and refugees in Baghdad telling their story to rulers too divided to answer. Your line was: a city in grief. Did you stop for a breath for a place in pain? Day nine hundred fifty-six.

As if he were being driven to his death. That, in one account, is how a young officer later described riding with his uncle's army to Egypt. He hadn't wanted to go. His name was Yusuf, son of Ayyub, from a Kurdish family that served the Turkish ruler of Syria, Nur al-Din. He would become known by an honorific, a title of praise: Salah al-Din, the righteousness of the faith. Some in the west learned to call him Saladin. Yesterday's refugees had named the problem: a divided people. The reluctant officer would spend his life on it. Today: Salah al-Din.
screen: `A RELUCTANT YOUNG OFFICER.` → `YUSUF, SON OF AYYUB.` → `THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: In Egypt, the Fatimid caliphs still ruled from Cairo, the city you met earlier this month. Salah al-Din's uncle became their vizier and soon died, and the post passed to the young Yusuf. Then he did something quiet and enormous. He had the Friday sermon in Egypt said in the name of the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, not the Fatimid one. The Fatimid line came to an end, and Egypt's Friday prayer named the Sunni caliph in Baghdad. When Nur al-Din died, Salah al-Din moved into Syria and, over years of bargaining and battle, brought Damascus, Aleppo and other cities under his rule. Now Egypt and Syria answered to one ruler. Not everyone welcomed him. Some of Nur al-Din's family and followers saw a servant taking his master's lands, and said so. His biographer, the judge Ibn Shaddad, who served beside him, paints a man who prayed, listened to hadith read aloud, wept easily, and gave away so much that he left almost nothing behind at his death. Biographers can love their subjects, so it's fair to hold that portrait a little loosely. Whatever else drove him, the work of his life, as these sources tell it, was bringing divided lands under one rule. The Qur'an has a line for that hope. In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A Kurdish officer, serving a Turkish lord, uniting Arab lands. The kurdish sultan.
screen: `THE FATIMID CALIPHATE ENDS.` · `EGYPT AND SYRIA UNDER ONE RULER.` · `IBN SHADDAD'S PORTRAIT.` · `HOLD FAST, ALL OF YOU TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE KURDISH SULTAN.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about unity. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where people you belong to are divided: a family that has stopped talking, a community split over something, friends on two sides of a quarrel. Don't try to solve it. Just see it clearly. Who is on each side? What do they still share? Now ask one honest question: what small thing could you do to bring two of them a little closer, without forcing anyone? If you pray, you can say the line: hold fast, all of you together, and do not separate. If you don't, simply hold the picture of them together. The bell holds the time.
Salah al-Din. Yusuf, son of Ayyub, the Kurdish officer who ended Fatimid rule in Egypt and united Egypt and Syria. His title means the righteousness of the faith. Today's word.
Your line: the kurdish sultan. Today, do one small thing to close a gap between people you care about: a message, an invitation, a kind word passed along. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

957.title: Jerusalem, 1187
957.hook: Salah al-Din retakes Jerusalem and lets many ransom out or leave in peace
957.howItsDone: Muslims retell Salah al-Din's taking of Jerusalem in sermons, books and classrooms, and the release of people who could not pay the ransom is often told as an example of mercy in victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Salah al-Din, who brought Egypt and Syria under one rule. Your line was: the kurdish sultan. Where did you see something pulled together that had been split apart? Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

The city has surrendered. Inside the walls, families are counting coins on kitchen tables. The terms, as the sultan's own secretary records them, are plain: each person may pay a ransom, take their goods and walk out of the gate within a set time. Some can pay. Some can't, and they know it. Out at the gate, the clerks sit with their lists, and everyone is waiting to see what the man who has just won will do about the people who have nothing to hand over. That man is Salah al-Din, and the city is the one Arabic calls the holy. Today's word: Jerusalem.
screen: `THE CITY SURRENDERS.` → `A RANSOM TO WALK OUT.` → `WHAT ABOUT THOSE WHO CAN'T PAY?`

segments.voice: In Arabic, Jerusalem is usually called al-Quds, the holy. It's the city of the Aqsa mosque, linked with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his night journey, and the hadith collections report that the believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the qiblah turned to Mecca. The Crusaders had held it, and Muslim chroniclers remembered the day they took it as a day of killing. So when Salah al-Din's army stood at the walls, payback might have been expected. What the accounts describe instead is a surrender on terms. Imad al-Din, the sultan's secretary, who was there, writes of the ransom and the gate. And then the part beyond the terms. The accounts say the sultan's brother, al-Adil, asked for a group of the poor as a gift, and set them free. They say Salah al-Din released others himself, among them the old, and let widows go. They also say that those who could not pay and were not freed were taken captive. That's worth saying out loud. Mercy came, and it didn't reach everyone. It was a choice made at a gate, by people, imperfectly. Why does the story keep being told? Because it sits close to a teaching in the Qur'an. In surah an-Nahl, the believers are told that if they punish, the punishment must match the wrong done to them, no more. And then: if they bear it patiently, that is better. In surah ash-Shura, the same turn: an injury may be answered with its like, but whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with Allah. The Qur'an allows a fair answer. It praises the pardon. Winning is the moment when that teaching costs the most, because winning is when you could.
screen: `AL-QUDS — THE HOLY.` · `A RANSOM AT THE GATE.` · `THOSE WHO COULD NOT PAY.` · `PARDON IS BETTER, THE QUR'AN SAYS.` · then, large: `MERCY IN VICTORY.`

segments.voice: The practice: show mercy in winning. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind somewhere you're ahead right now. An argument you won. A colleague who slipped up. A sibling who owes you an apology. A game, a deal, a debate in the group chat. Notice the pull to press it, to say the last word, to make sure they know. Then choose one small mercy you could show: let the point drop, let them keep their dignity, leave the final message unsent. If you pray, you can ask Allah for a soft heart in the moment you could be hard. If you don't, simply hold that person in mind for a while with some kindness. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem. In Arabic, al-Quds, the holy. The city Salah al-Din took back, where a ransom was set at the gate and some who couldn't pay walked out free. Today's word.
Your line: mercy in victory. Today, when you come out ahead, even in something small, give the other person a way to walk out with their dignity. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: The Mongols
958.hook: armies from the steppe sweep through Central Asia and Persia
958.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, from surah al-Baqarah, when they hear of a death or any loss, and Friday sermons sometimes close with supplications for people suffering war.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem, a ransom at the gate, and some who couldn't pay set free. Your line was: mercy in victory. When you came out ahead, did you leave someone their dignity? Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

A caravan of merchants rides into a border town called Otrar, on the eastern edge of the lands of the Khwarazm-shah. They have come from the ruler of the steppe peoples, to trade. As the chroniclers tell it, the governor of the town accuses them of being spies and has them killed. An envoy comes to complain, and he is killed too. It's a quarrel over goods and pride on a frontier, the kind of thing a governor might expect to forget. It was not forgotten. What came after it is today's word: the Mongols.
screen: `MERCHANTS RIDE INTO OTRAR.` → `KILLED AS SPIES.` → `IT WAS NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: The Mongols were peoples of the steppe, the wide grasslands north of China, horsemen who had been brought under one ruler, Chinggis Khan. After Otrar, their armies came west. They swept through Central Asia, through Bukhara and Samarkand, cities of mosques, markets and scholars, and on into Persia. The chronicles describe cities that resisted and were emptied, and cities that opened their gates and were spared, and they are hard reading. One historian, Ibn al-Athir, was writing a great history of the world in Mosul when the news arrived. He tells us that he held back from writing this part for a long while, because he could not bear to. And when he did write it, he says he wished he had died before it happened and been forgotten, words that echo Mary's cry in surah Maryam. A historian whose job was to write everything down, saying he would rather not have lived to write this. That's where today's line comes from: the storm from the east. It's a picture, not a weather report. It's how it felt to people who had no way to stop it. So what does a believer say when the news is that bad? You met the words at Jerusalem's fall; here is where they come from. In surah al-Baqarah it describes those who, when misfortune strikes them, say, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." In Arabic: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Muslims say it at a death, and at any loss or bad news, large or small. It doesn't explain the storm. It doesn't pretend it isn't happening. It simply says who we belong to while it passes over.
screen: `RIDERS FROM THE STEPPE.` · `BUKHARA, SAMARKAND, PERSIA.` · `A HISTORIAN WHO COULDN'T WRITE IT.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND TO HIM WE RETURN.` · then, large: `THE STORM FROM THE EAST.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember those who suffer war. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place where people are living through war right now. Not the maps or the arguments about it. The people: a grandmother who can't leave, a child who has learned the sound of planes, a doctor who hasn't slept. Let one of them be as clear as you can. If you pray, you can ask Allah for their safety, and for help to reach them. If you don't pray, simply keep them in mind for the whole sit, and don't look away early. The bell holds the time.
The Mongols. Horsemen of the steppe, united under Chinggis Khan, whose armies swept through Central Asia and Persia. Today's word.

Your line: the storm from the east. Today, do one practical thing for people living through war: give to a relief fund, write to someone who has fled one, or learn the name of one town that is suffering now. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Baghdad, 1258
959.hook: Baghdad falls, the caliph is killed, and chronicles say the Tigris ran dark with ink from books
959.howItsDone: Muslims treat copies of the Qur'an with care, keeping them clean and high, and the fall of Baghdad is remembered in histories and classrooms as a loss of lives and of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mongols, riders from the steppe, and a historian who could barely bring himself to write it. Your line was: the storm from the east. Did you do one practical thing for people living through war? Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

What color is a river after a library has been thrown into it? Later chroniclers had an answer, and it's the line people still repeat. The Tigris, they wrote, ran dark with the ink of the books washed off their pages. Whether that happened exactly as they say, historians argue. But nobody had to invent the grief behind it. The storm from the east had reached the city of the caliphs, a city of mosques, markets, hospitals and libraries, sitting on that river. Today's word is the city: Baghdad.
screen: `WHAT COLOR IS THE RIVER?` → `DARK WITH INK, THEY WROTE.` → `THE CITY OF THE CALIPHS.`

segments.voice: Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, the city of the House of Wisdom, where scholars had gathered and books had been copied and translated. When the Mongol armies came west, a prince named Hulagu, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, led them toward it. The city was besieged. The walls were breached. The chronicles say the caliph, al-Musta'sim, went out to the Mongol camp to surrender, hoping to save his people. The city was sacked anyway, and the caliph was killed. The accounts differ on how he died, and on almost every number, so we'll leave the numbers where they are, in dispute. Then there's the river of ink. Notice what people chose to remember. Not only the dead, though they mourned the dead. They remembered the books. Why would that be the picture that lasts? Because of where Islam begins. The first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in surah al-'Alaq, are a command to read, and they say of Allah, in Pickthall's English: "Who teacheth by the pen." A whole civilization had grown up around that pen: the Qur'an copied by hand, hadith written down, law, poetry, medicine, maps. To lose the books could feel like having the pen itself knocked out of their hand. And yet, the story didn't end there. Copies existed in other cities. Scholars carried what they knew in their memories. People who could write went on writing. The river of ink is a picture of loss. It's also a picture of what a people treasured, because you only grieve like that for something you loved.
screen: `THE CITY OF THE HOUSE OF WISDOM.` · `THE CALIPH GOES OUT, AND IS KILLED.` · `THEY REMEMBERED THE BOOKS.` · `WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `THE RIVER OF INK.`

segments.voice: The practice: protect a book. If you can, pick one up now: a copy of the Qur'an, a family Bible, a grandmother's recipe notebook, a school book with someone's name inside the cover. Hold it. Feel its weight. Think about who wrote it, who copied or printed it, who kept it until it reached you. Then give it one small act of care: wipe the dust off, mend a torn page, move it somewhere dry and high. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the pen and those who carried it. If you don't, simply hold the book a moment longer before you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Baghdad. The city of the Abbasid caliphs on the Tigris, sacked by Hulagu's army, its caliph killed, and its books, the chronicles say, thrown in the river. Today's word.
Your line: the river of ink. Today, look after one book or one piece of writing that matters to someone, and if it's been forgotten on a shelf, read a page of it. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.
